passages.text: In July 2025, the British government announced plans to lower the voting age for all elections in the United Kingdom from eighteen to sixteen. The change would not be wholly new. Sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds were already permitted to vote in elections for the Scottish Parliament and the Welsh Senedd, as well as in local elections in those two nations. Supporters contended that young people who can work, pay taxes, and join the armed forces at sixteen deserve a say in how they are governed, and that voting early helps form an enduring habit. Critics retorted that most sixteen-year-olds are still in school and may be too easily swayed, and some suspected that the governing party expected to gain from the reform.

For centuries in the ancient Mediterranean world, the most prestigious hue was a deep purple produced in the city of Tyre, in what is now Lebanon. The dye came from sea snails, and thousands of them had to be crushed to yield a small amount, which made the hue extraordinarily expensive. Wearing it became an emblem of power. In Rome, purple stripes and borders on their clothing marked senators and magistrates, and later emperors endeavored to reserve the finest shades for themselves. The association between purple and royalty outlived the dye itself, which fell into disuse after the fall of Constantinople in 1453. In 1856, a young English chemist named William Perkin accidentally produced a purple synthetic dye, and purple clothing at last became affordable to ordinary people.

Pisa's renowned bell tower started leaning within a few years of the start of its construction in 1173. The ground beneath it consists of soft clay and sand, and the foundation was far too shallow for such a heavy structure. Work then stopped for nearly a century, and the pause presumably saved the tower: the soil had time to compress and consolidate before more weight was added. Later builders endeavored to compensate by making the upper floors marginally taller on the leaning side, so the tower is curved. By the late twentieth century, the tilt had grown so perilous that the tower was closed. Engineers then excavated soil from beneath the higher side, reducing the lean by about 40 centimeters, and the tower reopened in 2001.

Self-checkout machines spread rapidly through supermarkets in the 2000s and 2010s, promising shorter lines and lower labor costs. In recent years, however, several large retailers in the United States and Britain have curtailed the number of machines in some stores or limited them to customers buying only a few items. Store managers have reported higher rates of theft and scanning blunders at the machines, and many customers resent doing work that employees once did for them. Supporters retort that the machines remain popular with shoppers who are buying a handful of items and prize speed over conversation. The debate suggests that automation does not invariably save as much money as it first appears to, notably when its concealed costs are counted.

[A] For more than a decade, technology companies promised that self-driving cars were (a) <u>imminent</u>, and for more than a decade the promise slipped. That pattern has finally begun to change. In several American cities, including Phoenix, San Francisco, and Los Angeles, residents can now open an app and summon an automobile with no one in the driver's seat, paying a fare much as they would for an ordinary taxi. In China, fleets of driverless taxis operate in parts of Wuhan and other large cities. What was only recently an experiment has become, in certain neighborhoods, an unremarkable part of daily life.
[B] Supporters point first to safety. Human drivers are weary, distracted, and occasionally drunk, and road accidents kill more than a million people worldwide each year. A machine never checks its phone. Operators have released data indicating that their vehicles are involved in fewer injury crashes per mile than human drivers in the same cities, although independent researchers note that such comparisons are difficult to make fairly. Supporters also contend that driverless taxis could offer independence to elderly and disabled people who cannot drive themselves.
[C] Critics are less enthusiastic. The vehicles still meet situations they handle poorly, such as atypical construction zones or police officers directing traffic by hand, and in those moments remote staff may need to (b) <u>intervene</u>. Emergency crews in some cities have complained that stalled vehicles blocked their path. Labor unions, meanwhile, warn that millions of people who drive for a living, from taxi and delivery drivers to long-haul truckers, could eventually lose their jobs. To them, hailing the technology now seems (c) <u>premature</u>.
[D] Regulators face a difficult balancing act. Regulations that are too stringent could stall a technology that may one day prevent many deaths; regulations that are too loose could let companies test unfinished systems on public thoroughfares, leaving ordinary pedestrians to bear the risk of any (d) <u>defect</u> in the software. Some governments have responded by permitting driverless taxis only in limited zones, expanding them step by step as safety records accumulate. Most observers concur that wider use is now (e) <u>inevitable</u>. The open question is how quickly it should come, and who should decide.

[A] In 1989 the American sociologist Ray Oldenburg popularized the term "third place" to designate the informal gathering spots that exist apart from the home, the first place, and the workplace, the second. Cafés, barbershops, taverns, and neighborhood bakeries were his canonical examples. What distinguished them, he contended, was not what they sold but what they permitted: people of disparate backgrounds could drop in uninvited, linger without being hurried, and converse with acquaintances (a) <u>they might never meet</u> elsewhere. Oldenburg also underscored that such venues are egalitarian: within them, a factory worker and a bank manager meet as peers, and social rank counts for less than wit or good humor. The ambience is playful rather than solemn, and the genuine allure is the company of the regulars rather than the coffee or beer on the counter.
[B] Oldenburg maintained that such places performed inconspicuous but indispensable work for democracy. Conversation among neighbors, he argued, cultivates the loose ties of trust (b) <u>that</u> enable communities to cooperate when crises arise. In aggregate, such modest bonds constitute a form of social capital that no institution can readily manufacture. Regulars register when someone is absent; shopkeepers know which elderly patron lives alone. These relationships are seldom profound, but their very casualness renders them effortless to form and (c) <u>surprisingly durable</u>.
[C] Many commentators lament that third places are in precipitous decline; suburban development, which separates homes from shops by lengthy drives, (d) <u>have made</u> spontaneous encounters more elusive. Escalating rents squeeze out independent cafés, and the chains that supplant them are frequently engineered for rapid takeaway rather than leisurely conversation. The internet provides a surrogate of sorts, though online forums seldom convene people who disagree in the way a crowded counter once did.
[D] Not everyone shares this bleak prognosis, however: some researchers point to new kinds of gathering places, from community centers (e) <u>reinvented</u> as hubs for clubs and classes to climbing gyms and board-game cafés that appeal to young adults. Whether these will assume the same civic function remains to be seen. What seems evident is that third places do not endure by accident; they depend on zoning ordinances, affordable rents, and proprietors willing to let customers linger longer than is strictly profitable.

[A] Long before notebooks were affordable, educated people cultivated their memories with a technique now known as the method of loci. According to an ancient anecdote, the Greek poet Simonides was the sole survivor when the roof of a banquet hall collapsed, and he was able to identify the crushed guests by recalling where each had been seated. Whether or not the tale is apocryphal, Roman teachers of rhetoric erected an entire system on its central insight: memory adheres to places.
[B] An orator preparing an address would envision a familiar edifice and deposit a vivid image representing each point of the argument in a separate chamber. During the oration, he proceeded through the edifice in his mind, retrieving the images in their prescribed sequence. Because speeches were customarily delivered without notes, the capacity to (a) <u>articulate</u> a protracted argument fluently hinged on such training. Roman handbooks advised making the images arresting, even grotesque or violent, since commonplace pictures were readily forgotten. Modern readers who encounter the bizarre illustrations in extant memory manuals often struggle to (b) <u>decipher</u> them. Writing existed, of course, but manuscripts were costly and cumbersome to consult, so a disciplined memory remained the principal repository of knowledge.
[C] Medieval scholars elaborated the art still further: monks committed vast portions of scripture to memory, and teachers deployed imagined buildings, gardens, and ladders to classify what their pupils absorbed. Such discipline was believed to (c) <u>foster</u> not only recall but also moral and spiritual contemplation, and an erudite reader would (d) <u>meditate</u> on a text by pacing deliberately through its images. Memory, in this conception, was not a storeroom but a ____: a site for thinking, not merely for keeping.
[D] The printing press gradually eroded this culture, for once books grew inexpensive and indexes ubiquitous, many writers came to regard memorization as antiquated, and the elaborate art was disparaged as a (e) <u>trivial</u> trick. It has never entirely vanished, however; competitive memory champions still rely on imagined edifices to recall lengthy sequences of playing cards or digits, and empirical studies indicate that novices instructed in the method can markedly augment their recall within a few weeks of practice.

[A] Most people are serenely confident that they would notice if their interlocutor were suddenly replaced by someone else. Experiments on what psychologists term change blindness suggest otherwise. (Ⅰ) Our conviction that we perceive a rich and meticulously detailed world at every instant is partly an illusion. The brain retains far less than it seems to, filling the gaps with expectations about what is presumably there, and so long as nothing salient appears altered, we tacitly assume that nothing has changed. Perception, in other words, is less a faithful transcript of the world than a plausible reconstruction of it.
[B] In a celebrated study from the late 1990s, a researcher approached pedestrians on a college campus to ask for directions. Midway through the exchange, two men hauling a large door barged rudely between them. (Ⅱ) Concealed behind the door, the researcher was surreptitiously replaced by a different person, who calmly resumed the conversation. Approximately half of the pedestrians failed to notice that they were now addressing a stranger, even though the two experimenters differed conspicuously in height, attire, and voice. (Ⅲ) Those who did detect the switch tended to be close in age to the experimenters.
[C] Change blindness is not a sign of poor eyesight or of unusual carelessness. (Ⅳ) Attention is a finite resource, and the brain must incessantly discern what merits tracking. In a perfunctory exchange about directions, a stranger's identity may simply not seem pertinent, so the particulars of his face are never encoded firmly enough to be compared with what ensues. Film editors have long exploited this vulnerability: continuity errors, such as a glass that is brimming in one shot and empty in the next, routinely elude most viewers.
[D] The phenomenon carries tangible consequences: drivers may overlook a motorcycle that emerges while they glance at a mirror, and eyewitnesses may confidently misidentify a suspect in a police lineup. (Ⅴ) Researchers contend that the most reliable safeguard is a measure of humility about our own perception. The sensation of having seen everything is no proof that nothing has changed, and consequential judgments should not rest on that sensation alone, a caveat that is anything but academic in courtrooms and on highways alike.

[A] In June 2023, smoke from hundreds of wildfires burning across Canada drifted south and turned the sky over New York City a hazy orange. For a few days, the city recorded some of the worst air quality of any major city in the world, and residents who had never given wildfires a thought found themselves scrambling for masks. The episode was dramatic, but it was not unique. As fire seasons grow longer and more intense, smoke is becoming a (a) <u>chronic</u> problem for communities that may lie hundreds or even thousands of kilometers from the nearest flame.
[B] The main peril comes from fine particles known as PM2.5, which are less than 2.5 micrometers across, approximately thirty times thinner than a human hair. Unlike larger particles, which are trapped in the nose and throat, these can penetrate deep into the lungs and even pass into the bloodstream. Short-term exposure can (b) <u>aggravate</u> asthma and other breathing problems, and studies have linked smoky days to surges in emergency-room visits for heart and lung conditions. Some research suggests that particles from wildfire smoke may be more detrimental, gram for gram, than those from other sources, conceivably because burning homes and vehicles release a mixture of toxic chemicals along with the burning vegetation.
[C] The burden does not fall evenly. Outdoor workers, such as farm laborers and construction crews, often cannot stay inside on smoky days without forfeiting wages. Older adults, young children, and pregnant women are notably (c) <u>sensitive</u> to polluted air; children, for example, breathe more air relative to their body weight than adults do, and their lungs are still developing. And people living in poorly sealed housing may breathe virtually as much smoke indoors as outdoors, while wealthier households can retreat behind closed windows and run air purifiers.
[D] Public health officials have begun to respond. Many regions now issue smoke forecasts, much as they issue weather warnings, and some cities open "clean air shelters" with filtered air during the worst episodes. Researchers underscore that simple measures can (d) <u>diminish</u> exposure considerably: a well-fitting N95 mask filters out most fine particles, and a homemade purifier built from a box fan and a filter can clean the air in a single room. Such steps cannot (e) <u>substitute</u> for longer-term endeavors to manage forests and slow the warming that feeds larger fires, but they can safeguard people while those endeavors take effect.

[A] In the mangrove swamps and river mouths of Southeast Asia and northern Australia lives a diminutive fish with a most peculiar method of hunting. The archerfish lurks just beneath the surface until it detects an insect alighting on foliage that overhangs the water. It then presses its tongue against a groove in the roof of its mouth and abruptly contracts its gill covers, (a) <u>firing</u> a jet of water that can dislodge the prey from its perch at a distance of more than a meter. By the time the stunned insect strikes the surface, the fish is usually poised directly beneath it, ready to engulf its quarry.
[B] The feat is more formidable than it appears. Because light bends, or is refracted, as it passes from air into water, an insect viewed from below appears displaced from its actual position. An archerfish, however, (b) <u>adjust</u> its aim to compensate for this optical distortion, and seasoned adults seldom miss. The fish can even modulate the jet so that the water gathers into a compact mass just before it reaches the target, delivering a more forceful blow than a uniform stream would.
[C] Archerfish are also unusually adept learners. In controlled laboratory experiments, juvenile fish that had (c) <u>watched</u> skilled companions hit moving targets subsequently sharpened their own aim, apparently by learning vicariously, through observation, rather than through trial and error alone. In another study, fish (d) <u>trained</u> to spit at one of two photographs of human faces continued to single out the correct face even when it was embedded among dozens of unfamiliar ones, an astonishing aptitude for an animal whose small, comparatively rudimentary brain lacks the specialized regions that mammals employ to recognize faces.
[D] Researchers scrutinize the archerfish not merely for its own sake but for what it reveals about how nervous systems solve difficult computational problems. Its hunting entails the rapid, simultaneous estimation of distance, angle, and timing, and its proficiency implies that intricate skills need not depend on a large brain. Scientists caution against drawing sweeping conclusions from a single species, but the little fish (e) <u>has become</u> a favorite model in debates over the nature of animal cognition.

[A] In August 2021, the United Nations Environment Programme announced that leaded gasoline for cars had finally vanished from service stations worldwide, after Algeria, the last country still selling it, exhausted its remaining supplies. In the early 1920s, American engineers had discovered that adding a compound dubbed tetraethyl lead to gasoline stopped engines from knocking, a damaging form of uneven combustion. The additive was cheap and efficacious, and within a few decades it was being burned in vehicles on every inhabited continent.
[B] Its perils were apparent from the start. Workers at plants producing the additive in the 1920s suffered hallucinations, and several perished. Lead is a poison that accumulates in the body, and it is notably detrimental to children, whose developing brains are vulnerable even to small amounts. Health authorities now assert that no level of lead exposure is known to be safe; even low levels are associated with poorer attention and lower scores on intelligence tests. Yet for decades the industry insisted that the quantities released from automobile exhausts were harmless, and few independent scientists scrutinized the question closely.
[C] That began to change after the geochemist Clair Patterson, while endeavoring to measure the age of the Earth, found lead contamination everywhere in his laboratory and in the environment around it. His later measurements demonstrated that lead levels in modern people and in recent layers of polar ice were far higher than in earlier times, and he spent years contending that leaded gasoline was the main source. As countries phased out the additive, beginning in the 1970s, average levels of lead in children's blood fell drastically. In the United States, they dropped by more than 90 percent.
[D] Economists have since endeavored to estimate what the change was worth. One analysis backed by the United Nations estimated that ending leaded gasoline prevents more than a million premature deaths each year and saves trillions of dollars, largely by safeguarding children's health and future earnings. Some researchers have gone further, linking the decline of lead to falling crime rates, although that claim remains contested. Whatever the exact figures, the narrative offers a sobering lesson: a substance can spread across the entire planet long before anyone ____.

[A] On Saturday mornings the municipal pool was the dominion of children, shrieking and splashing and gliding through the water with the effortless grace of fish, and of one middle-aged man who had never learned to swim. I was that man: for decades I had eschewed beaches and pools, concocting elaborate excuses whenever friends broached the prospect of an excursion, and the (a) <u>embarrassed</u> silence that greeted my refusals had become a familiar companion. The phobia had originated, as nearly as I could reconstruct it, on a childhood afternoon when a breaker overturned me at the seaside and pinned me beneath the surf for what felt like an eternity. When my daughter enrolled in lessons, however, I recognized that I had no wish to bequeath her my dread along with my surname.
[B] The instructor, a retired lifeguard named Mrs. Ortiz, did not commence with strokes or breathing drills. For the first two weeks she required of me only that I float, (A) ____ by her hand at first and subsequently by nothing at all. I detested the regimen, for floating, it transpired, demanded the very surrender I had (b) <u>devoted</u> my entire life to evading: to cease struggling and trust that the water's buoyancy would sustain me. Every primal reflex urged me to thrash, clutch, and hold my head aloft, and each time I yielded to those reflexes, I sank.
[C] By the third month I could manage a laborious, clumsy length of the pool. It was hardly a (c) <u>magnificent</u> achievement, and the children in the adjacent lane overtook me with casual ease. Yet I emerged from the water that evening feeling inexplicably (d) <u>blissful</u>, as though I had relinquished a burden I had shouldered for decades. Neither my daughter nor her friends (B) ____ impressed, of course; to them, swimming was as mundane as walking.
[D] What endured was not the swimming itself but the counterintuitive lesson of those initial weeks. So much of my apprehension, I came to understand, had stemmed from my own (e) <u>rigidity</u>, the reflexive impulse to combat whatever eluded my control. I still recall that pool whenever a predicament seems to demand ever more strenuous effort. On occasion, I remind myself, the more prudent course is to lie back, loosen my grip, and let the water perform its quiet work.

In October 2025, Sanae Takaichi became the first woman to serve as prime minister of Japan. Earlier that month she had won the leadership of the Liberal Democratic Party, which has governed Japan for most of the period since the 1950s, but becoming prime minister still required a vote in parliament. Her path was complicated when the party's long-time coalition partner, Komeito, withdrew from the government, and the Liberal Democrats reached a new agreement with another party in order to secure enough support. Her election drew attention abroad partly because women remain a small minority in Japan's parliament and in senior business positions. Observers noted, however, that her policy views were largely conservative and that her rise did not by itself signal broader change.

The arrangement of letters on most English keyboards, known as QWERTY after the first six letters of the top row, dates back to typewriters of the 1870s. A popular narrative holds that the layout was designed to slow typists down so that the machine's metal arms would not jam. Historians have questioned this account. Some contend that the arrangement owed more to the needs of telegraph operators, who transcribed Morse code, than to any desire to curtail speed. Whatever its origins, the layout has proved remarkably durable. Alternative designs that claim to be faster have existed for nearly a century, yet few people embrace them, because the cost of relearning outweighs the modest benefit for most users.

In 1898, the psychologist Norman Triplett discerned that cyclists rode faster when racing against others than when riding alone against the clock. In a follow-up experiment, children winding fishing reels tended to work faster when another child was doing the same task beside them. Later researchers dubbed this social facilitation: the presence of others can enhance performance. The effect, however, has a catch. In the 1960s, the psychologist Robert Zajonc contended that an audience raises arousal, which helps on simple or well-practiced tasks but hurts on arduous or unfamiliar ones. An expert violinist may perform at her best in a packed hall, whereas a novice may falter on passages she plays effortlessly in private.

Rainbows are produced by water droplets acting as minuscule prisms. Sunlight enters a drop, is bent, bounces off the drop's inner surface, and is bent once more as it exits. Red and violet light are bent to marginally unequal degrees, and this small difference fans the sunlight out into separate hues. An observer can see the bow only when the sun shines from behind and rain is falling ahead, and the colored arc invariably sits approximately 42 degrees away from the shadow of the observer's head. Because each person's eyes collect light from their own particular droplets, two friends standing apart are looking at two distinct rainbows. The ground usually conceals the bottom of the arc, yet pilots flying above the clouds occasionally see a rainbow as a full ring.

[A] Few institutions seem as timeless as the restaurant, yet in its modern incarnation it is scarcely more than two and a half centuries old. Before the late eighteenth century, travelers in France could dine at inns or purchase prepared dishes from caterers, but they customarily sat at a communal table, consumed whatever the host happened to be serving, and paid a fixed price. Food was frequently presented on large shared platters, and latecomers might find the platters all but depleted. The notion of selecting from an array of dishes, at a private table, at an hour of one's own choosing, would have struck most diners as decidedly peculiar.
[B] The word "restaurant" originally denoted not a place but a food: a rich broth believed to (a) <u>cure</u> exhaustion and restore the vigor of the feeble and the infirm. In the 1760s, Parisian entrepreneurs began opening establishments that sold these restorative broths to customers who wished to eat sparingly, and the shops themselves came to be dubbed restaurants. Unlike inns, they allowed patrons to (b) <u>consult</u> a menu, sit at small separate tables, and come and go at any hour. Their earliest clientele often comprised people of delicate health, or those who wished to appear so.
[C] The French Revolution is often credited with disseminating the new institution; according to a popular account, cooks who had served aristocratic households lost their employers and opened restaurants of their own. Historians now deem this narrative (c) <u>exaggerated</u>, since restaurants already existed in Paris before 1789. The upheaval did, however, help render dining out a fashionable pursuit for an expanding middle class, who could now display their discernment in public as only nobles once had. Proprietors swiftly discovered that a reputation for culinary excellence could attract throngs.
[D] What the restaurant offered, above all, was a new kind of ____. Diners were no longer guests obliged to accept whatever they were given; they were customers entitled to choose. The menu, with its catalogue of dishes and prices, transformed eating into an expression of personal taste and gave cooks an incentive to (d) <u>refine</u> their dishes in competition with rivals. A diner could also remain (e) <u>anonymous</u> in a crowded room, eating among strangers without owing anyone conversation. Much of modern urban life, from the café to the food court, grew out of that deceptively simple change.

[A] For years, European industries complained that the fight against climate change left them at a disadvantage. Factories in the European Union must buy permits for every tonne of carbon dioxide they emit, while competitors in countries without such regulations face no comparable cost. Economists warned of "carbon leakage": production, and the emissions that come with it, might simply relocate abroad, (a) <u>leaving</u> the planet no better off and Europe poorer. Without some correction, Europe's climate policy could end up exporting jobs rather than curtailing pollution. Some heavy industries, such as steel and cement, seemed notably likely to relocate.
[B] The EU's answer is the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, customarily shortened to CBAM. Under the scheme, importers of certain carbon-intensive goods, namely iron and steel, aluminum, cement, fertilizers, electricity, and hydrogen, must pay a charge (b) <u>based on</u> the emissions released in producing them, approximately matching what a European manufacturer would pay. Importers will cover the charge by buying certificates whose price follows that of carbon permits inside the EU. A transitional phase that began in October 2023 required importers only to report those emissions; importers become liable for the charge on goods imported from 2026. If an exporting country already (c) <u>impose</u> a carbon price of its own, the amount paid there can be deducted.
[C] Supporters see the mechanism as a way to safeguard European industry while nudging other countries toward cleaner production. A steelmaker in Asia or Africa that wants to keep selling to Europe now has a reason to measure, and eventually to cut, its emissions. Several governments, (d) <u>having watched</u> the EU's plans develop, have begun designing carbon-pricing systems of their own, partly so that the revenue stays at home rather than flowing to Brussels. In this sense, the measure may spread carbon pricing far beyond Europe's borders.
[D] Critics, however, raise several objections. Exporters in developing countries contend that the measure is protectionism dressed in green clothing, and that it punishes nations which contributed least to historical emissions. Companies of every size complain about the paperwork, since calculating the emissions embedded in a single shipment can be extraordinarily complicated. Others fear retaliation, since trading partners might answer with taxes of their own on European goods. Some economists also doubt how much the charge will curtail global emissions, (e) <u>given</u> that producers may simply send their cleanest goods to Europe and their dirtiest to other markets.

[A] In 1609, Galileo Galilei was a mathematics professor at the University of Padua, esteemed by colleagues but far from affluent. His salary was modest, and he supplemented it by taking in student lodgers and selling instruments. Like many scholars of his time, he aspired to escape these burdens by finding a powerful (a) <u>patron</u> at one of Italy's princely courts. That year he heard of a Dutch device that made distant objects appear closer, and he quickly built enhanced versions of his own, grinding the lenses himself until his instruments could magnify objects about twenty times.
[B] Turning his telescope to the night sky in early 1610, Galileo saw mountains on the Moon, countless stars invisible to the naked eye, and four small points of light circling Jupiter. He rushed his findings into print in a short book, The Starry Messenger, and made a shrewd decision: he named the four moons the Medicean Stars, in honor of Cosimo II de' Medici, the young Grand Duke of Tuscany, and his brothers. Before the book appeared, Galileo had been relatively (b) <u>obscure</u> outside Italian academic circles; within months he was renowned across Europe, and copies of the book were eagerly sought in distant cities.
[C] The strategy worked. Later that year Cosimo appointed him chief mathematician and philosopher to the Grand Duke, a position that freed him from teaching and permitted him to (c) <u>obtain</u> a generous salary for life. Galileo's (d) <u>aspiration</u> had long been to devote himself to research rather than to the routine duties of a professor, and the court post seemed to fulfill it at last.
[D] Historians note that patronage shaped early modern science in ways that are easy to overlook. Scholars competed for the attention of princes, and discoveries could serve as gifts that brought prestige to both giver and receiver. It would be a blunder, however, to (e) <u>attribute</u> Galileo's achievements to flattery alone; his observations were meticulous and could be checked by anyone with a good telescope. The episode demonstrates that even revolutionary science depended on money, status, and the favor of the powerful.

[A] "It isn't broken, only tired," the old man said, turning the little red car over in his fingers. My son, who was six, had been inconsolable since the train left the city, and our fellow passengers had begun to signal their (a) <u>disdain</u> for the noise with conspicuous sighs. One wheel of his cherished toy had worked loose, and I possessed nothing with which to mend it. The man across the aisle, who had been reading unobtrusively for most of the journey, (A) ____ his newspaper and asked whether he might inspect it.
[B] He extracted a hairpin from his coat pocket, bent it into a minuscule hook, and worked at the axle with a gravity that (b) <u>captivated</u> my son. He labored in silence, holding the car close to his spectacles, while my son nestled against my arm and tracked every deft movement. Within ten minutes the wheel rotated freely; my son's tears stopped at once, and he spent the remainder of the trip racing the car along the windowsill, murmuring engine noises under his breath. When I attempted to express my gratitude, he merely shrugged and remarked that he had spent his working life repairing radios, and that small machines seldom required anything more than a modicum of attention.
[C] We disembarked at different stations, and I never learned his name, and for years I presumed that my son had long since forgotten the episode; he was so young, and the toy had been lost long ago. Then, at his university graduation, he alluded unprompted to the man on the train. He said it was the first time he (B) ____ that a stranger could help simply because help was needed, without anticipating any recompense. The memory, he confided, had (c) <u>shaped</u> the way he treated people he would never encounter again.
[D] I have since become persuaded that the kindnesses we remember are seldom grand. They are unassuming, (d) <u>incidental</u> gestures performed by people who anticipate no thanks and who depart before any can be offered. Such acts entail virtually no cost, yet their effects can be (e) <u>cumulative</u>, passing unobtrusively from one person to the next in ways that no one can trace. I think of the man whenever I am tempted to avert my gaze from a stranger's modest predicament and persuade myself that it is none of my concern.

[A] It is widely assumed that the long summer vacation in American schools exists because children were once needed to help on family farms. The explanation is tidy, endlessly repeated, and largely erroneous, for in the agrarian communities of the nineteenth century, children's labor was most indispensable during spring planting and autumn harvest, and rural schools typically convened their sessions in winter and summer, when fieldwork was less onerous. Summer, in other words, was frequently a season of schooling in the countryside rather than a respite from it.
[B] The modern summer break originated instead in the cities. In the early nineteenth century, many urban schools operated virtually year-round, with brief recesses interspersed throughout the calendar. As reformers sought to standardize education, they contended that such protracted school years overtaxed children's minds and bodies, a concern that some physicians of the era echoed in alarming terms. Sweltering heat in congested classrooms, (a) <u>which</u> had no air conditioning, made learning arduous, and affluent families routinely (b) <u>left</u> the cities for cooler retreats in July and August. A uniform summer vacation incrementally emerged as a compromise between the urban and rural calendars, and by the early twentieth century it (c) <u>has become</u> the national norm.
[C] The break has proved remarkably resilient, but it has also attracted sustained criticism. Researchers have long documented that students tend to forfeit some academic skills over the summer, a pattern colloquially dubbed the summer slide, and that the losses (d) <u>appear</u> larger for children from low-income families, whose summers may offer fewer books, camps, and trips. More recent studies have disputed the magnitude and consistency of the effect, but apprehension about it has galvanized experiments with shorter breaks distributed more evenly across the year.
[D] Such calendars remain the exception rather than the rule, largely because parents organize employment and childcare around the long break, tourism and summer camps depend on it, and many instructors prize it as an interval for recuperation and professional development. The history of the summer vacation thus affords a broader lesson: customs that seem to have self-evident practical origins are occasionally explained after the fact by narratives that are more gratifying than accurate, and those narratives can make an arrangement appear far more intractable than it (e) <u>really is</u>.

[A] Every few months, it seems, another company announces that it has been hacked. Telecommunications carriers, retailers, hospitals, and government agencies have all reported breaches in recent years, some exposing the personal information of tens of millions of people at once. Names, phone numbers, addresses, passwords, and in the worst cases national identification numbers and medical records have ended up for sale in online criminal markets. For the individuals affected, the consequences may not appear for months: a fraudulent loan application, an unfamiliar charge on a card, or a convincing phone call from someone who already knows a great deal about them.
[B] Several trends have made breaches both more prevalent and more damaging. Companies collect far more data than they did a generation ago, often keeping it long after it has served its purpose. Ransomware gangs, which lock up a victim's computer systems and demand payment, increasingly steal data as well, threatening to publish it unless they are paid. And because many organizations rely on the same outside software providers, a single weakness in one extensively used program can expose thousands of customers at once. Security experts often assert that attackers need to succeed only once, while defenders must succeed every time.
[C] Once data has leaked, it cannot be called back. A password can be changed, but a date of birth or a fingerprint cannot. This is why many experts contend that the most efficacious protection is ____: information that was never gathered, or that was deleted when it was no longer needed, cannot be stolen. Some privacy laws now require companies to justify the data they hold and to dispose of what they do not need, though enforcement varies extensively from country to country.
[D] Regulators have also begun to elevate the cost of carelessness. In several jurisdictions, companies that fail to safeguard customer data now face fines calculated as a share of their annual revenue, and executives may be required to explain their failures in public hearings. Customers, for their part, are advised to use distinct passwords for distinct services, to turn on two-step verification, and to treat unforeseen messages asking for personal information with suspicion. None of these measures guarantees safety. Together, however, they can make an individual a harder target, and in the economics of cybercrime, attackers tend to move on to easier ones.

[A] Most people who fail to reach their objectives do not lack good intentions. They resolve to exercise, to save money, or to complete a report early; somehow, the moment for action slips by. The predicament is not confined to the weak-willed; it afflicts virtually everyone at some juncture. The psychologist Peter Gollwitzer has devoted decades to investigating this chasm between intention and action, and he has proposed a strikingly simple remedy. (Ⅰ) Rather than merely deciding what they wish to attain, people should stipulate in advance precisely when, where, and how they will act.
[B] Gollwitzer dubs such plans "implementation intentions," and they adopt an if-then format: "If it is 7 a.m. on a weekday, then I will put on my running shoes." (Ⅱ) The plan links a specific situation to a specific behavior, so that when the situation arises, the behavior ensues with little need for fresh deliberation. In effect, the person delegates control of the action to the environment and no longer has to remember the goal and summon willpower at precisely the opportune moment; the situation does the reminding. Dozens of studies have tested the technique. (Ⅲ) Meta-analyses that aggregate the results of many of them have found that it substantially enhances the likelihood that people actually execute their plans.
[C] The technique seems notably beneficial for people who struggle with self-control, and for objectives that are easily forgotten or deferred, such as taking medication or attending a medical screening. (Ⅳ) It can also help people resist entrenched habits. Someone endeavoring to curtail snacking, for example, might resolve: "If I feel hungry in the afternoon, then I will eat an apple." The plan does not eliminate the craving, but it furnishes a ready response before the craving can prevail.
[D] Implementation intentions are no panacea. (Ⅴ) They work best when the underlying objective is one a person genuinely wishes to attain, and they can backfire if plans are so inflexible that a single disruption derails everything. Still, their appeal lies in their modesty: rather than exhorting people to become more disciplined in general, they ask them only to determine, ahead of time, what they will do when the moment arrives. Some researchers recommend coupling such plans with a candid appraisal of the obstacles likely to stand in the way.

[A] Visitors to Venice marvel at its palaces and churches, but few contemplate what lies beneath them. The city rests on a cluster of small islands in a shallow lagoon, where the substrate consists largely of soft mud and sand. To build on such unstable ground, Venetian builders over many centuries drove millions of wooden piles, hewn from trees such as alder, larch, and oak, deep into the lagoon floor, and then laid platforms of timber and stone atop them. Beneath the largest edifices, the piles were driven so densely that they constitute a virtually solid mass.
[B] At first glance, the method seems doomed to failure, since timber left in water ordinarily rots within years. The piles beneath Venice, however, have survived for centuries because they are entirely submerged in waterlogged mud, an environment so deficient in oxygen that the fungi responsible for most decay cannot (a) <u>flourish</u>. Over time, minerals in the water have (b) <u>permeated</u> the wood, rendering parts of it harder and better able to (c) <u>withstand</u> the immense load above. The builders appear to have grasped this empirically long before anyone could elucidate it scientifically.
[C] The system is by no means invulnerable: analyses of piles extracted during repairs demonstrate that anaerobic bacteria, which tolerate scant oxygen, do gradually soften the outer layers of the wood. Wherever the water level drops and air reaches the piles, decay accelerates drastically. The graver (d) <u>threat</u>, however, now emanates from above the waterline, where salt water that inundates the city with mounting frequency corrodes brick and stone. As it rises by capillary action into the walls, the salt crystallizes and gradually crumbles the masonry.
[D] Since 2020, a system of mobile barriers at the inlets to the lagoon has been raised during exceptionally high tides to repel the sea. The barriers have spared the city several floods, but they are costly to operate, and scientists warn that rising sea levels may necessitate deploying them so frequently that the lagoon's ecology deteriorates. Some experts have proposed more radical interventions, from elevating pavements to injecting water deep underground to lift the city marginally. Venice's foundations have endured for a millennium; whether the city above them can (e) <u>secure</u> its future for another century is a far more open question.

In January 2025, European climate scientists corroborated that 2024 had been the warmest year since reliable records began, and the first calendar year in which the global average temperature was more than 1.5 degrees Celsius above the level before industrialization. The figure garnered attention because 1.5 degrees is the more ambitious limit named in the Paris Agreement. Scientists underscored, however, that the agreement refers to warming averaged over two decades or more, so a single hot year does not by itself mean the target has been missed. Part of the heat came from El Niño, a natural pattern of warm water in the Pacific Ocean that raises global temperatures for a time. Most of it, they added, reflected the long-term warming driven by greenhouse gases.

The seven-day week is so ubiquitous that it seems natural, yet unlike the day, the month, or the year, it corresponds to no evident cycle in nature. Its roots lie in the ancient Near East. The Babylonians ascribed special significance to the number seven, and the Jewish tradition of a weekly day of rest gave the seven-day cycle an enduring religious meaning. The Romans, who had long used an eight-day market cycle, incrementally embraced the seven-day week, and in 321 the emperor Constantine made Sunday an official day of rest. Endeavors to replace the system have not lasted. Revolutionary France introduced a ten-day week in the 1790s, but it proved profoundly unpopular and was abandoned about a decade later.

Instructors often tell students to stop doodling and pay attention, presuming that drawing in the margins is a sign of a wandering mind. A study published in 2009 hints that the reverse can occasionally hold. Participants listened to a long, tedious telephone message full of the names of people and places. One cohort filled in printed squares and circles with a pencil during the recording, while a second cohort sat without any task. Afterward, in a surprise memory test, the doodlers recalled about 29 percent more information. The researcher hypothesized that a simple drawing task may keep the mind from drifting into daydreams, holding attention at a level just high enough to stay engaged with a boring task. The finding does not mean, however, that every kind of drawing helps.

Sharks are often depicted as living fossils, but the label is deceptive. The earliest sharks appeared more than 400 million years ago, long before the first trees grew on land, yet modern sharks are not unchanged relics. Over that immense span, they have diversified into more than five hundred species, from the plankton-eating whale shark, the largest fish alive, to small species that glow faintly in the deep sea. What has persisted is a durable basic design: a skeleton of flexible cartilage rather than bone, keen senses that can detect minuscule electrical fields, and teeth that are continually replaced throughout life. Today, however, overfishing has put a large share of shark species at risk of extinction.

[A] Visitors to old European churches are occasionally told that medieval window glass is thicker at the bottom because glass is genuinely a liquid that has been flowing slowly downward for centuries. The narrative is charming and extensively repeated, but physicists and historians of glassmaking concur that it is spurious. Its appeal (a) <u>derives</u> partly from a genuine puzzle. Glass is not a crystal like ice or quartz, and so it occupies an atypical place among the familiar states of matter, which is enough to make the notion of an exceedingly sluggish liquid sound plausible.
[B] In a crystal, atoms are arranged in a regular, repeating pattern. In glass, they are frozen in a disordered arrangement resembling that of a liquid, because molten glass cools too quickly for an orderly structure to form. Scientists hence dub glass an amorphous solid. Calculations suggest that at room temperature ordinary window glass would need far longer than the age of the universe to flow noticeably. Ancient Roman glass vessels in museums show no sign of sagging, and old telescope lenses still focus light without the slightest (b) <u>distortion</u>.
[C] The uneven windows have a more mundane explanation. Many medieval glaziers made flat glass by spinning a blob of molten glass into a large disc, a method that produced panes of uneven thickness. When the panes were cut and installed, the thicker edge was often placed at the bottom, conceivably for stability. Yet (c) <u>verification</u> of the flowing-glass theory would require that virtually every old window be thicker at the bottom, and that is not what meticulous surveys find: some panes are thicker at the top or along one side.
[D] The persistence of the myth demonstrates how a vivid explanation can (d) <u>interfere</u> with the spread of a correct but less colorful one. Still, the puzzle that gave rise to it is genuine. Why some liquids, when cooled, freeze into a glass instead of a crystal, and what exactly happens to their atoms as they do, remains one of the (e) <u>fundamental</u> open questions in the physics of solids.

[A] Aviation is among the most intractable industries to decarbonize. Automobiles can run on batteries, but batteries powerful enough to propel a long-haul jet across an ocean would be so heavy that they would leave scant room for passengers or cargo. Hydrogen-powered aircraft remain, for now, largely experimental. For the foreseeable future, therefore, much of the industry has pinned its hopes on sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF: jet fuel (a) <u>made</u> not from crude oil but from feedstocks such as used cooking oil, agricultural residues, or even carbon captured from the air.
[B] The appeal of SAF is that it can be blended with conventional kerosene and burned in existing engines without substantial modification, so airlines need not await a new generation of aircraft. Its carbon dioxide emissions at the point of combustion are comparable to those of fossil fuel, but because the raw materials (b) <u>absorbing</u> carbon from the atmosphere as they grew, or would otherwise have been discarded, its emissions over its entire life cycle can be dramatically lower, by as much as 80 percent according to some estimates.
[C] Governments have begun to mandate its use. Under a European Union regulation, fuel supplied at EU airports must contain at least 2 percent SAF from 2025, rising to 6 percent in 2030 and 70 percent by 2050. The principal obstacles are supply and price. SAF still accounts for well under 1 percent of the jet fuel consumed worldwide, and it typically commands a price several times that of conventional fuel. The supply of used cooking oil, the cheapest feedstock, is finite, and critics fear that surging demand could spur fraud, (c) <u>with</u> virgin palm oil passed off as waste, or divert crops away from food production.
[D] Proponents contend that mandates are precisely what is needed to (d) <u>bring</u> costs down, much as government subsidies once helped make solar panels affordable; producers investing in new refineries need assurance that buyers will materialize. Skeptics retort that fuel is only part of the problem, since aviation also warms the climate through contrails and other non-carbon effects, and that the most dependable way to curb its emissions in the short term may simply be to fly less. Both camps concur, however, that much of the additional cost will eventually (e) <u>be passed</u> on to passengers in the form of higher fares.

[A] Central Asia's cotton boom hinged on water, and most of that water came from two great rivers. For centuries, the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya had carried snowmelt from distant mountains across the desert into the Aral Sea, once the fourth-largest lake on Earth. In the 1960s, Soviet planners resolved to turn the arid plains of Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan into vast cotton fields, cultivating a crop so lucrative that it was dubbed "white gold." Engineers excavated thousands of kilometers of canals, diverting so much of the rivers' flow that only a trickle still reached the sea. Within a few decades, the lake had begun to retreat at an alarming pace, exposing a salt-crusted seabed.
[B] Irrigating through open earthen canals was relatively inexpensive, but it squandered water in one of the most parched regions on Earth. Many canals were unlined, so a substantial share of what they carried seeped into the sand or evaporated before reaching any field. As the sea shrank, its salinity soared and most of its native fish vanished, devastating a fishing industry that had employed tens of thousands. Former ports such as Moynaq were left stranded many kilometers from the water, their rusting trawlers marooned in the sand. Winds now sweep salt and dust from the dry seabed across nearby towns and farmland, and that dust may carry residues of the pesticides once sprayed on the cotton fields.
[C] The medical picture remains murky, partly because reliable health data from the region are scarce and were long collected by officials with little incentive to publicize bad news. Since cotton is often marketed as a natural, wholesome fiber, the region's record has proved problematic for clothing brands. For years, many of them shunned Uzbek cotton because of the forced labor used in the harvest, a practice that international monitors later reported had largely ended. Governments, meanwhile, confront competing pressures, since cotton promises export revenue and employment at a time when these economies need both, and abandoning the crop altogether would devastate rural livelihoods.
[D] Engineers have demonstrated that partial recovery is possible: in 2005, Kazakhstan completed a dam, financed partly by the World Bank, that sealed off the smaller northern part of the sea, whose level then rose enough for fish and fishermen to return. Lining canals and adopting drip irrigation could also curtail losses elsewhere, although that will take years and considerable investment, since the region's irrigation network is vast and aging. The larger southern basin, by contrast, has largely dried up. Until such approaches mature, the region's cotton economy will carry an uncomfortable irony: ____.

[A] Pronounce a simple word, such as "door," aloud thirty times in succession, and something curious is likely to transpire. (Ⅰ) Somewhere along the way, the word begins to sound peculiar, even meaningless, as though it were an arbitrary noise in a foreign tongue rather than a familiar component of ordinary discourse. Psychologists term this experience semantic satiation, a label coined in the early 1960s by the researcher Leon Jakobovits James, who made it the subject of his doctoral dissertation.
[B] Why does it occur? One prominent explanation invokes a kind of neural fatigue. (Ⅱ) When we hear or utter a word, a pattern of neural activity binds its sound to its meaning. Reiterating the word over and over triggers that pattern again and again, and the response incrementally attenuates, much as a muscle tires after repeated exertion. For a short interval the sound continues to register, but its tether to meaning grows tenuous. (Ⅲ) The effect is transient, however; after a brief respite, the word regains its ordinary sense.
[C] Researchers have documented analogous effects beyond spoken words: scrutinizing a written word for a prolonged period can make its spelling look erroneous, and viewing the same face or shape repeatedly can induce a comparable erosion of recognition. (Ⅳ) Such findings suggest that satiation is not an idiosyncrasy of language alone but a pervasive feature of how the brain responds to repetitive stimulation. Even a beloved song can forfeit some of its charm when it is played on a loop for an entire afternoon.
[D] The phenomenon has even been harnessed for practical ends. Some therapists have experimented with asking anxious clients to repeat a distressing word until it sheds some of its emotional potency, and there is tentative evidence that the technique can alleviate distress, though further research is warranted. Most people, however, encounter satiation only inadvertently: a student copying a difficult word many times before a spelling test may abruptly doubt whether it is spelled correctly at all. (Ⅴ) The experience is a modest reminder that meaning does not reside inside words themselves but is incessantly reconstructed by the mind.

[A] The envelope had lain wedged behind a kitchen drawer for nearly forty years when Mina discovered it while clearing out her late aunt's apartment. It was addressed in pencil to a woman she had never heard of, stamped but never posted. Inside was a single page, folded twice and (A) ____ in a meticulous, slanting hand that Mina recognized at once as her aunt's. She sank onto the bare floor of the emptied kitchen and read it before she had quite resolved whether she ought to.
[B] The letter was an act of contrition: her aunt, who had invariably struck Mina as the most (a) <u>placid</u> of people, recounted a quarrel with a close friend over a borrowed sum of money. She confessed that she had (b) <u>belittled</u> her friend's explanation and that pride had hardened a petty misunderstanding into an enduring estrangement. She wrote that she had begun the letter many times and abandoned it on each occasion, unable to summon words that did not ring like excuses. Her handwriting grew cramped toward the bottom of the page, as if her resolve had been running out as fast as the space.
[C] Mina spent two weeks endeavoring to trace the friend; old directories proved fruitless, but a former neighbor recollected the name and directed her to a nursing home on the outskirts of the city. The woman there was ninety-one, frail but lucid. When Mina proffered the letter, the old woman read it twice in silence and then chuckled softly. She said that she (B) ____ waiting for that letter for most of her life, and that she had forgiven Mina's aunt decades earlier without ever (c) <u>revealing</u> it to anyone.
[D] Mina had feared that her visits might seem (d) <u>intrusive</u>, but the old woman received them with palpable pleasure, and Mina returned several times before the old woman died the following spring. Neither the aunt nor her friend, it appeared, had ever wholly ceased to dwell on the other. They conversed at length about her aunt as a young woman, quick-tempered and magnanimous, whom Mina had never known. Mina still retains a copy of the letter, not as a record of a (e) <u>breach</u> between two friends, but as a reminder of how long an unspoken word can linger, and of how little it might have taken to utter it.

[A] For centuries, readers of the Iliad and the Odyssey puzzled over a curious feature of Homer's style. Certain phrases recur again and again: dawn is almost always "rosy-fingered," the sea "wine-dark," and Achilles "swift-footed." To modern readers, such repetition can seem (a) <u>rudimentary</u>, even tiresome. Some scholars suspected negligent copying by later scribes; others revered the phrases as poetic ornaments without asking why there were so many of them or why they appeared in such predictable places.
[B] In the 1920s and 1930s, a young American scholar named Milman Parry proposed a distinct explanation. The repeated phrases, he contended, were tools of oral composition. A singer composing aloud in front of an audience could not stop to search for the perfect word. He needed a repertoire of ready-made phrases that would (b) <u>adhere</u> to the strict rhythm of the line, and the epithets supplied exactly that: each fit a particular position in the meter, so that a name could be completed in whatever space remained.
[C] To test the notion, Parry and his assistant Albert Lord traveled to Yugoslavia, where traditional singers still performed long epic songs without writing. They recorded singers who could perform thousands of lines and found that no two performances of the same song were identical. The singers were not reciting a fixed text; they were recomposing the narrative each time from familiar phrases and scenes, much as Homer's epithets suggested. One singer produced a song of more than twelve thousand lines. For many scholars, the findings were a (c) <u>revelation</u>. Parry died young in 1935, and Lord later set out their conclusions in a renowned book, The Singer of Tales.
[D] Parry's work transformed the study of early literature. It suggested that the Homeric poems emerged from a long tradition of oral performance before being written down, and it altered how scholars approach epics from many cultures. Debate continues over exactly how and when the poems took their written form, and whether a single poet of genius shaped them. Yet few now regard the repeated phrases as indications of carelessness. They are, instead, (d) <u>potent</u> reminders that literature was performed long before it was read, and of the skill that permitted singers to (e) <u>sustain</u> a performance for hours.

[A] Standard economic theory treats money as fungible, or fully interchangeable. A dollar is a dollar, whether it derives from wages, a gift, or a fortuitous find, and it should be spent with identical prudence. Real people, the economist Richard Thaler observed, do not conduct themselves this way; they sort money into mental categories, such as rent money, vacation money, or free money, and they (a) <u>treating</u> each account by its own rules. Thaler christened this proclivity mental accounting.
[B] Mental accounting elucidates many otherwise perplexing choices: a person who wins a small prize at a casino may gamble it away with abandon, since it feels like the house's money rather than his own. Families occasionally keep money in a savings account yielding negligible interest while carrying credit card debt at a far steeper rate, (b) <u>because</u> the savings are earmarked for a special purpose. In one celebrated example, people (c) <u>who</u> lose a theater ticket are less willing to purchase a replacement than people who lose an equivalent amount of cash on the way to buy one, even though the loss is identical.
[C] Such behavior is not wholly irrational, since labeling money can be a valuable instrument of self-control. A household that allocates a fixed sum for groceries each week, or a worker who treats a tax refund as savings rather than discretionary income, may (d) <u>be</u> better off than one that treats all its money as a single undifferentiated pool. Some researchers contend that mental accounts function like fences, insulating long-term objectives from short-term temptations.
[D] Businesses and governments have become adept at exploiting these tendencies. Retailers promote gift cards, which customers tend to spend more liberally than cash. Some governments have found that labeling a cash transfer for a particular purpose, such as children's education, alters how families spend it, (e) <u>even though</u> nothing precludes them from diverting the money elsewhere. Lottery winners and recipients of an unforeseen bonus often spend that money quite differently from their regular income as well. Money, it seems, carries the labels we affix to it.

[A] In the late nineteenth century, the port neighborhoods of Buenos Aires and Montevideo were crowded with newcomers: immigrants from Italy and Spain, migrants from the countryside, and the descendants of enslaved Africans. Many lived in cramped tenements where conditions could be (a) <u>oppressive</u>, with whole families sharing a single room around a common courtyard. Out of this confluence of peoples and musical traditions, a new music and dance emerged: the tango.
[B] Early tango drew on European dance forms, the Cuban habanera, and rhythms associated with Afro-Argentine communities. It was played in dance halls, cafés, and on street corners, at first with guitar, flute, and violin, and later with the bandoneon, a kind of accordion brought by German immigrants. Respectable society regarded the dance as vulgar, associating it with poverty and nightlife, and many middle-class families forbade their children to learn it. The close embrace of the dancers seemed to (b) <u>unleash</u> everything that courteous manners tried to restrain.
[C] Around 1913, the tango abruptly became a sensation in Paris. Affluent young Argentines living in Europe had brought it with them, and Parisians, who found it (c) <u>exotic</u> and daring, crowded into dance schools for lessons, held afternoon tango teas, and even bought clothing in a fashionable tango orange. The craze quickly spread to London, New York, and Berlin, where newspapers debated whether the dance was an innocuous amusement or a threat to public morals. Ironically, the upper classes of Buenos Aires, who had scorned the dance for years, embraced it only after ____.
[D] In the decades that followed, tango became an emblem of national identity in both Argentina and Uruguay, and its music evolved into a sophisticated art form that composers eventually carried into the concert hall. In 2009, UNESCO formally recognized the tango as part of humanity's living heritage, an honor that the two countries share. Its history demonstrates how a form born on the margins of society can (d) <u>transcend</u> its origins, and it remains a (e) <u>compelling</u> example of how cultural prestige occasionally travels home by way of foreign approval.
